summary: Federal AI use is publicly inventoried; GAO audits it, and the state legislatures writing AI law are tracked on this site.

analysis.body:
The U.S. Government Accountability Office has produced the most detailed public record of federal AI deployment to date, finding that twenty of twenty-three major agencies reported approximately 1,200 current and planned AI use cases spanning activities such as analyzing drone photographs, processing large datasets, identifying border activities from cameras and radar, and targeting scientific specimens for planetary rovers. NASA and the Department of Commerce reported the highest number of use cases among the agencies surveyed. Despite the breadth of reported activity, GAO found that most of these use cases remained in the planning phase rather than in active production, with roughly 200 instances where agencies reported actually using AI operationally at the time of review.

GAO also identified significant gaps in the quality of agency reporting itself. Only five of the twenty agencies that submitted inventories provided comprehensive information for each reported use case, while the remaining fifteen had instances of incomplete or inaccurate data. Two agencies even included AI applications that were later determined not to be AI at all. Without accurate inventories, GAO concluded, the government's ability to manage its AI use will be constrained by the very data it relies on to do so.

Compliance with federal AI requirements has been uneven across agencies. Ten of the twenty-three agencies audited had implemented all AI requirements specific to them, twelve had implemented some but not all, and one was exempt. The Office of Management and Budget had not yet developed government-wide guidance on how agencies should acquire and use AI, a gap GAO identified as preventing consistent management of AI risk and benefit. The General Services Administration established an AI Center of Excellence and the Department of Commerce created a plan for AI technical standards, representing two of the more complete implementations. The President's fiscal year 2023 budget request included 1.8 billion dollars for nondefense research and development investment in AI, signaling continued federal financial commitment even as governance frameworks lag behind.

On the legislative side, 3,277 AI bills have been tracked across 53 jurisdictions in the United States, updated daily from LegiScan and maintained on this site's AI Laws section. The volume of state-level activity reflects a regulatory environment that is moving quickly and unevenly, with individual states filling gaps that federal guidance has not yet addressed. Internationally, Oxford Insights scores nearly every country through its Government AI Readiness Index, evaluating policy capacity, governance, infrastructure, and public-sector adoption as a standard cross-national comparison, while OECD.AI tracks national AI strategies and ethical frameworks across member and partner countries, giving policymakers a structured view of where their own approaches stand relative to peers.

Stanford HAI's annual AI Index provides a cross-sector view noting that technical capabilities are improving, investment is accelerating, and adoption is spreading, but that the frameworks needed to govern and evaluate AI are falling behind. The 2026 edition specifically highlighted a widening gap between what AI can do and how prepared institutions are to manage it, a characterization that fits the federal picture GAO documented precisely. For any organization deciding whether to deploy AI in or alongside government contexts, the practical implication from these sources is that the technology is present and expanding but that governance infrastructure, acquisition guidance, and workforce classification remain works in progress, making compliance readiness as important a consideration as technical capability.
